how-much-cam-do-i-owe-based-on-square-fo.text:
← CAM Reconciliation Check

How much CAM do you owe based on square footage?

Common-area-maintenance share is a straight ratio: your square footage divided by the building's total rentable square footage, multiplied by the building's annual CAM expenses. Here is that arithmetic worked out for six suite sizes in the same building, holding total area and annual expenses at the calculator's own defaults.

Modeled CAM by suite size in a 10,000 sq ft building

$120,000 annual CAM expenses, 10,000 sq ft total rentable area. Arithmetic only — not a lease interpretation or a bill.
Suite sizeArea shareModeled annual CAMModeled monthly CAM
250 sq ft2.50%$3,000.00$250.00
500 sq ft5.00%$6,000.00$500.00
1,000 sq ft10.00%$12,000.00$1,000.00
2,500 sq ft25.00%$30,000.00$2,500.00
5,000 sq ft50.00%$60,000.00$5,000.00
8,000 sq ft80.00%$96,000.00$8,000.00

Area share is tenant area ÷ rentable area. Modeled annual CAM is annual expenses × area share. Modeled monthly CAM is the annual figure ÷ 12. Every column comes from the same two inputs held constant across the table.

The area-share ratio does all the work here: every suite size in this table sits at exactly $12 of modeled annual CAM per square foot, because $120,000 ÷ 10,000 sq ft is a constant rate. That is what makes the relationship proportional — a 2,500 sq ft suite owes exactly ten times what a 250 sq ft suite owes, because it is exactly ten times the area, nothing else.

What this table cannot tell you is whether your own lease actually uses a straight area ratio. Some leases fix a tenant's share by exhibit rather than by current measured area, some carve out anchor tenants or vacant space from the denominator, and some cap increases or exclude categories entirely — any of which moves the real number away from this arithmetic.

Open the calculator and enter your building's actual expenses, total area, and your suite's area to see your own modeled share, plus a variance check against what you were actually billed. Nothing you enter is uploaded.

This page is arithmetic, not legal, tax, financial, or real-estate advice. It does not tell you what your lease requires or whether a bill is correct.

Common questions

How do I calculate how much CAM I owe based on my square footage?

Your modeled CAM share is your tenant square footage divided by the building's total rentable square footage, multiplied by the building's annual CAM expenses. On a 10,000 sq ft building with $120,000 in annual CAM expenses, a 1,000 sq ft suite — 10.00% of the building — models to $12,000 a year, or $1,000 a month. A 2,500 sq ft suite in the same building is 25.00% of the building and models to $30,000 a year ($2,500 a month).

Does a bigger suite always mean a proportionally bigger CAM bill?

Yes, in this arithmetic model — area share is a straight ratio of your square footage to the building's total, so doubling your area exactly doubles your modeled share. Going from a 1,000 sq ft suite to a 2,000 sq ft suite in the same 10,000 sq ft building doubles the area share from 10.00% to 20.00% and the modeled annual CAM from $12,000 to $24,000. What can break that proportionality in a real lease is a fixed pro-rata share stated in an exhibit, exclusions or caps that apply differently by tenant, or a base-year stop that only some tenants have — none of which this model assumes for you.

PRIVATE LEASE-MATH WORKSHEET

Check the CAM math before you argue about the bill.

Model a tenant's common-area-maintenance share, subtract credits, and see exactly where the billed amount differs. No lease or expense data leaves this browser.

Statement figures

Occupancy gross-up (optional)

Leave blank unless the lease has a gross-up clause. Most net leases let a landlord gross up the occupancy-sensitive share of CAM — utilities, janitorial, the costs that track how many suites are occupied — to what it would have cost at a stated target occupancy, usually 95%, when the building actually ran below that. Fixed costs (management fee, roof reserve, and similar) are never grossed up, which is why only the variable share is adjusted here.

The link carries these eight figures in the part of the URL after the #, which browsers never send to a server. Whoever you send it to — a landlord, a tenant, a broker, your accountant — opens this worksheet already filled in and can change any input to test their own version of the number.

Transparent result

Tenant area share
Gross-up adjustment

Modeled tenant share
Net billed after credits
Variance: modeled less billed

A positive variance means the modeled share is higher than net billed. A negative variance means net billed is higher. This is arithmetic, not a conclusion about what the lease allows.

Review checklist

Use these prompts to compare the statement with your records. They do not replace professional review.

    Use it safely

    Everything runs locally. We count only anonymous feature events in local storage, never people, content, IPs, or cookies. A share link is the one thing that carries your figures off this device: they ride in the part of the URL after the #, which browsers never send to any server, but anyone holding the link can read them — so treat it exactly like the downloaded worksheet.

You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for meeting any obligation it helps prepare for. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

    Reconciling processor payouts against the bank feed instead of a landlord's CAM bill? The payment reconciliation workbench matches Stripe, Square, or PayPal payouts to bank deposits by amount and date and lists what does not match — nothing uploaded.

    Free and open source. If it caught a CAM reconciliation variance before you signed off, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

    Common questions

    How is the tenant's area share calculated?

    Tenant square footage divided by the building's total rentable area. On the defaults — a 1,000 sq ft suite in a 10,000 sq ft building — that is 10.00%. This is the pro-rata share most CAM clauses use, but some leases fix a share by exhibit instead of by current measured area; check the lease's own definition before treating the ratio as automatic.

    What does “modeled tenant share” mean, and how is it different from the billed amount?

    Modeled tenant share is annual CAM expenses multiplied by the area share — on the defaults, $120,000 × 10.00% = $12,000. The billed amount is whatever the landlord's statement actually charged, net of credits: $10,000 − $500 = $9,500 net billed. The variance ($12,000 − $9,500 = $2,500) is the arithmetic gap between what the area ratio alone would produce and what the statement actually asked for — it is a starting point for review, not proof of an error.

    What does a positive variance mean, and what does a negative one mean?

    A positive variance (modeled share above net billed, as in the $2,500 default) means the area-ratio math produces a bigger number than what was billed — worth checking that exclusions, caps, or a different pro-rata method in the lease account for the gap before assuming an undercharge. A negative variance means net billed is above the modeled share, which is the direction worth checking for an overcharge, an estimate true-up, or a category that should not have been included at all.

    What is a CAM gross-up, and when should I use it?

    A gross-up clause lets a landlord adjust the occupancy-sensitive share of CAM expenses (utilities, janitorial — the costs that track how many suites are occupied, not fixed costs like a management fee) up to what they would have cost at a stated target occupancy, usually 95%, when the building actually ran below that. Leave the gross-up fields blank unless your lease has this clause; entering the variable expense share and the actual and target occupancy percentages adds the adjustment to the modeled expenses before the area share is applied, and the worksheet shows the dollar amount added so it can be checked against the lease's own clause.

    What should I actually check before disputing a CAM bill?

    Three things in order: that the expense total and the statement cover the same lease year, that rentable and tenant area match the lease's own definitions (not just the current rent roll), and that every category on the statement is one the lease actually allows to be passed through. This tool only checks the arithmetic between those inputs — it does not read the lease and cannot tell you whether a category belongs on the bill.

    Does this replace a lawyer, accountant, or property manager?

    No. It is a private arithmetic worksheet for spotting a variance worth asking about. Whether that variance is allowed, owed, or worth disputing depends on the lease's own reconciliation clause, which only a qualified reviewer of the actual document can answer.

    Is my lease or expense data uploaded anywhere?

    No account and no network requests — the calculation runs in your browser and the downloaded worksheet and JSON record save straight to your device. Anonymous feature counts are local-only, optional, and the checkbox above turns them off.

    Can I send this reconciliation to the landlord, the tenant, or my accountant?

    Yes — “Copy a link to this reconciliation” produces a URL that reopens this page with all eight figures already entered, so the other side can change the rentable area, the expense total, or the gross-up target to whatever their own records say and watch the variance move. That is usually the more useful thing to send than a fixed worksheet, because a reconciliation argument is about the inputs. The figures travel in the part of the URL after the #, which browsers never transmit to a server, but they are readable by anyone the link reaches; share it the same way you would share the statement itself.

vs-square-footage-alone.html.text:
← CAM Reconciliation Check

This worksheet vs. reconciling CAM by square footage alone

Tenant square footage divided by the building's total, times annual expenses, is the whole calculation — unless the lease lets the landlord gross up the occupancy-sensitive share of expenses to a stated target occupancy. Skip that clause and an under-occupied building's CAM bill comes out understated.

What square footage alone gets you

Area share times annual expenses is correct, exactly, whenever the building ran at or above the lease's gross-up target occupancy for the statement period, or the lease carries no gross-up clause at all. Most of the CAM math genuinely is that simple: one ratio, one multiplication, done.

It stops being the whole answer the moment both of two things are true: the lease has a gross-up clause, and the building ran under the target occupancy that clause names — typically 95%. In that case, only the occupancy-sensitive share of expenses (utilities, janitorial, and similar costs that track how full the building is) gets adjusted upward to what it would have cost at full target occupancy; fixed costs like a management fee or a roof reserve are never touched. Area share alone has no way to apply that adjustment, so it reconciles against the expenses as billed and quietly leaves the gross-up out.

What this worksheet adds

It takes the same five statement figures — annual expenses, total rentable area, tenant area, billed amount, and credits — and three optional gross-up fields: what share of expenses is variable, the building's actual occupancy for the period, and the lease's target occupancy. Leave the three blank and it reproduces the area-only figure exactly. Fill them in and it grosses up the variable share before applying the area ratio, and shows the dollar amount that adjustment added.

Square footage aloneThis worksheet
Applies the area ratio to expenses exactly as billed, with no way to account for a gross-up clause. Grosses up the variable share of expenses to the lease's target occupancy before applying the area ratio, when the fields are filled in.
Gives one number regardless of how full the building actually was during the statement period. Reports the dollar adjustment the gross-up added, so it can be checked against what the lease's own clause allows.
Has no way to flag that an under-occupied building understates the modeled share without the clause applied. Shows the modeled share both ways, on request, from the same five base inputs.
Compares against a single billed figure with no record of the comparison. Computes a variance against net billed and a share link that hands the same numbers to a landlord, tenant, or accountant.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it runs entirely in your browser, and a share link carries only the numbers in the form — nothing is uploaded.

Same suite, one clause changes the number

Take this worksheet's own defaults: a 1,000 sq ft suite in a 10,000 sq ft building, $120,000 in annual CAM expenses. Read as pure square footage — 10.00% of the building — the modeled share is $12,000 a year, $1,000 a month. That is the whole answer if the building ran at or above target occupancy, or the lease has no gross-up clause.

Add a gross-up clause: 60% of expenses classed as variable, the building running at 75% actual occupancy against a 95% target. The variable share ($72,000) grosses up by a factor of 95 ÷ 75, adding $19,200 to the expense pool before the area ratio is applied. Effective annual expenses become $139,200, and the modeled tenant share rises to $13,920 a year, $1,160 a month — $1,920 a year more, 16% above the square-footage-only figure. Same suite, same total expenses, same area ratio. Only the occupancy clause changed the number.

Common questions

What's wrong with just using square footage share alone?

Nothing, if the building ran at or above the lease's gross-up target occupancy, or the lease has no gross-up clause at all -- area share times annual expenses is the whole calculation in that case. It goes wrong when the lease lets the landlord gross up the occupancy-sensitive share of expenses (utilities, janitorial -- costs that track how many suites are occupied) to what they would have cost at a stated target occupancy, usually 95%, and the building actually ran below that. Area share alone applies the ratio to the expenses as billed and never adjusts for the shortfall, which understates the modeled amount for a fully-tenanted year.

How much difference can the gross-up make in practice?

Using this worksheet's own defaults -- a 1,000 sq ft suite in a 10,000 sq ft building, $120,000 in annual CAM expenses -- square footage alone models the tenant's share at $12,000 a year, $1,000 a month. Add a gross-up clause with 60% of expenses classed as variable, the building running at 75% actual occupancy against a 95% target, and the modeled share rises to $13,920 a year, $1,160 a month -- $1,920 a year more, 16% above the area-only figure, from the same square footage and the same expense total.

How do I know if my lease has a gross-up clause?

Check the CAM or operating-expense reconciliation section of the lease itself for language about adjusting or grossing up expenses to a stated occupancy percentage. If that language is absent, area share alone is the correct calculation and this worksheet's optional gross-up fields should stay blank -- they default to a complete no-op (0% variable, 100% actual and target occupancy) so leaving them empty reproduces the area-only figure exactly.

Do I need my accountant's numbers to use this?

No. Five numbers already on the statement -- annual expenses, total rentable area, your tenant area, the billed amount, and any credits -- plus three optional gross-up fields if the lease has that clause. The worksheet does the area-share and gross-up arithmetic; nothing is uploaded, and a share link carries only the numbers you entered.
